task_context.problem_statement: Prove using a counting argument (combinatorial proof) that the number of ways to choose a committee of k people from a group of n people is the same as the number of ways to choose a subcommittee of n-k people to be left out. Specifically, show that C(n, k) = C(n, n-k).

messages.content: I'm working on this problem: 'Prove using a counting argument (combinatorial proof) that the number of ways to choose a committee of k people from a group of n people is the same as the number of ways to choose a subcommittee of n-k people to be left out. Specifically, show that C(n, k) = C(n, n-k).' I think the answer is just to use the formula n! / (k!(n-k)!) and show it's the same for both sides. Is that right?

While the formula certainly shows the values are equal, the problem specifically asks for a 'counting argument' or a 'combinatorial proof.' This means you need to explain why the two quantities are the same by describing a relationship between the sets being counted, rather than using algebra. How might you describe the process of picking a committee in a way that naturally identifies who is NOT on the committee?

Oh, I see. So I should say that for every group of k people I pick, there's a group of n-k people left over. So if I have 10 people and I pick 3, I've automatically picked 7 to stay home. Does that count as the proof?

You've identified the core intuition! To turn this into a formal combinatorial proof, you should explicitly describe a bijection. In other words, explain how every unique way to choose the committee of k corresponds to exactly one unique way to choose the group of n-k people. Can you phrase that more formally as a mapping between the two sets?

Okay, so I'll say: Let S be the set of all possible committees of size k. For every committee C in S, there is a corresponding set S \ C which contains exactly n-k people. Since this mapping is one-to-one, the number of ways to choose k people must be the same as choosing n-k people. Is that a complete proof now?

That logic is sound. To make it fully rigorous, you might want to explicitly state that the mapping is a bijection—meaning it's both injective and surjective. Why is it true that every possible group of n-k people corresponds to exactly one group of k people?
Because if you know exactly who was left out (the n-k people), there is only one possible group of people who could have been chosen for the committee (the remaining k people). So it works both ways.

Exactly. By showing that choosing the 'included' group is logically equivalent to choosing the 'excluded' group, you've provided a combinatorial argument. You've successfully moved from an algebraic verification to a conceptual proof.
